[Compute Cell Scheduling Records]
Compute Cell Scheduling Records
This document records how tasks were scheduled on small compute clusters. The workload and the machine
failures are real records from a production compute cell of about 12,500 machines (the Google cluster trace of
May 2011, clusterdata-2011-2, CC-BY 4.0): every task's submission time, job, priority, CPU and memory request
and run time, and every machine's capacity, failure time and return time, are taken from that trace (ids are
renamed). Where and when each task ran in the small cluster is not recorded in the trace: it is computed from
those records by the scheduling policy stated below, applied exactly.
The document is divided into chapters titled 'Cell window <NN>'. Each chapter is an independent run of one small
cluster over a window of 1200 seconds. Questions refer to a chapter by that title. Times are whole seconds from
the start of the window (time 0); the window covers times 0 to 1200.
Each chapter has four sections. 'Machines' lists the cluster's machines with their CPU and memory capacity, the
time a machine failed (if it did) and the time it returned (if it did). 'Task log' lists, in time order, every event of every
task from time 0 to the window end: submit, start, finish, evict and fail, with the task's job, priority, CPU and
memory request, run time, and the machine involved. 'Events' lists machine failures and returns, evictions and
restarts, and the longest waits. 'Queue at window end' gives the state after the events at time 1200: the tasks still
running (with their remaining run time) and the tasks still waiting, in queue order.
Tasks. A task belongs to a job and has a priority from 0 to 11 (higher is more important). Priorities 9 to 11 are the
production tier and priorities 0 and 1 the free tier. Each task requests an amount of CPU and of memory, which it
holds on one machine while it runs, and has a run time: once started it runs for exactly that many seconds and
then finishes, unless it is stopped first. The run time is given on every row of the task log, starting with the task's
submit row.
Scheduling policy. Every window starts with all machines empty and no task waiting. At every time at which

 time: once started it runs for exactly that many seconds and
then finishes, unless it is stopped first. The run time is given on every row of the task log, starting with the task's
submit row.
Scheduling policy. Every window starts with all machines empty and no task waiting. At every time at which
something happens, in this order:
1. Finishes. Tasks whose run time is over finish and free their CPU and memory.
2. Failures. Machines that fail at this time go down. Each task running on such a machine stops (a fail event) and
goes back to the queue.
3. Returns. Machines that return at this time come back, empty, with their capacity.
4. Submissions. Tasks submitted at this time join the queue.
5. Scheduling round. The waiting tasks are taken one at a time in queue order: higher priority first, then earlier
submission time, then lower task id. Each task, in turn:
a. First fit. The task starts on the first machine, in machine id order, that is up and whose free CPU and free
memory are both at least the task's requests (subject to the reservation rule in c).
b. Preemption. If it fits nowhere, no task holds a reservation yet in this round, and it is a production task, it may
evict free-tier tasks from one machine. It looks at the up machines in id order. On each it considers the free-tier
tasks running there, lowest priority first, then the most recently started first (then the higher task id first), and
evicts them one by one in that order until it fits; it takes the first machine where this works, evicting only as many
as needed there, and starts on it. If no machine works, nothing is evicted. An evicted task goes back to the queue
at once (it may start again later in the same round); it loses its progress and will run its full run time again.
c. Reservation and backfilling. The first task in the round that can start neither by a. nor by b. gets a
reservation: the earliest time at which it could start, computed from the run times of the tasks now running
(assuming no new submissions, failures or returns), on the first machine, in id order, where that earliest time is
reached. Every later task in the round may still start by first fit, but on the reserved machine only if it will finish no

chunks.path: Compute Cell Scheduling Records
chunks.text:
[Compute Cell Scheduling Records]
, computed from the run times of the tasks now running
(assuming no new submissions, failures or returns), on the first machine, in id order, where that earliest time is
reached. Every later task in the round may still start by first fit, but on the reserved machine only if it will finish no
later than the reserved time, or if its requests fit in what the reserved machine will still have free at the reserved
time after the reserved task's requests (and after other such starts on it in the same round). On the other
machines it starts as usual. Later tasks do not preempt. A task that would not fit on any up machine even if that
machine were empty gets no reservation and simply keeps waiting; the next task that cannot start may then get
the reservation.
Tasks stopped by an eviction or a failure keep their original submission time (and so their place in queue order)
and start again from the beginning. A task never moves while it runs.
Order of rows. Task log rows with the same time follow the steps above: finishes (by task id), failures (by
machine, then task id), submissions (by task id), then the scheduling round's starts and evictions in the order the
round makes them (each eviction just before the start that caused it).
Terms used in the Events section and in questions. A task's wait is the time from its submission to its first
start. A task is restarted when it starts again after an eviction or a failure. The number of evictions counts evict
events (one per evicted task). 'Running on a machine at time t' means running after all the events at time t.
The cluster and the workload. Each window has 8 machines, ids M01 to M08. Each is modelled on a real
machine of the cell (one of them is a machine that failed during the window in the trace) and has 1/8 of that
machine's recorded CPU and memory capacity. A failed machine returns at the time the trace records it coming
back, if that is within 6 hours; otherwise it does not return. The tasks are a sample of the real tasks submitted in
the cell during the window, chosen by this fixed rule: jobs submitted in the window are taken in a random order,
first up to 6 production jobs, then free-tier jobs until the offered load reaches 54%, then other jobs until it reaches
90% (a job that would push it above

chunks.text:
[Compute Cell Scheduling Records]
 in
the cell during the window, chosen by this fixed rule: jobs submitted in the window are taken in a random order,
first up to 6 production jobs, then free-tier jobs until the offered load reaches 54%, then other jobs until it reaches
90% (a job that would push it above 95% is skipped). A job contributes its first 4 tasks (16 for a free-tier job) that
finished normally in the trace and fit on at least one machine of the window. Offered load = the larger, over CPU
and memory, of the sum of request x run time inside the window over all tasks, divided by the cluster's total
capacity x the window length.
After the window. For questions about what happens after time 1200: no new task is submitted and no machine
fails after the window; a machine that is down returns at its listed return time (if any); the policy continues
unchanged from the state given in 'Queue at window end'.
Units. Times and run times in seconds. CPU and memory in units of 1/100,000 of the largest machine in the
original cell (the trace's normalised values, rounded to whole units).
Chapters in this document (itops_d01): Cell window 04, Cell window 07, Cell window 11, Cell window 18, Cell
window 22, Cell window 25.
